name: Vera Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Vera. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out of the yard by half seven in a rented white van, usually about 130 parcels on a weekday. The courier app gives me the route and I mostly ignore its order, because I know the flats on Station Road and which ones have a broken buzzer. I like the quiet hour before the schools let out. What wears me out is the app docking me for a late drop when the lift's been broken all week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you paid, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Per parcel, through the app, about 1.10 a drop, and they cut it from 1.25 last spring with one email. I live with my girlfriend Noor, she's a care worker on nights, so we pass each other at breakfast. We've got about three months of rent and bills put away, which feels like a lot until the van needs tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Fine, I can picture that easily enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the union group chat: the robots were never the problem, the per-drop rate is. If AI fizzles, the app is still the boss and still cuts our pay by email. I'd keep pushing for a proper minimum per hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing gets easier for me. The rate cut last spring already took about 60 a week off me, and the van rental went up in September. A world with no big AI change still has the app squeezing us a few cents at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my 130 drops and keep paying my union dues, which is 12 a month. I'd put 50 a week aside again, because we dipped into savings when the van's clutch went. And I'd go to the depot meeting in January about the new rates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, more than scared. It's the same grind, and I know the grind. I just don't see it getting any better on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the app is the boss. What does that look like on a bad day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month it flagged me for 14 late drops in a week because a block on Mill Lane changed its door code. Nobody to call, just a chat bot that says sorry. I got a warning that one more week like that and I'd lose the morning routes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the rate dropped again next year, which bill goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone contract goes to a cheaper one, then takeaways. Noor and I would stop the car insurance on her old car and sell it. Rent never goes, that's the line.

say: The **per-drop rate** is my problem, not robots, and the app cuts it by email whenever it likes.
Couriers need a **minimum per hour**, and I'd keep saying that in the union chat whatever AI does.
think: My pay is already **shrinking**: the rate cut took about 60 a week and the van costs more.
A world where AI fizzles still leaves the **app squeezing** me a few cents at a time.
do: Keep doing **130 drops** a day and keep paying 12 a month in union dues.
Save **50 a week** again to rebuild the cushion after the clutch repair.
Attend the **January depot meeting** about the new per-drop rates.
feel: **Tired** more than scared, because the grind is familiar and isn't getting better.
S0.quote: The robots were never the problem, the per-drop rate is. If AI fizzles, the app is still the boss and still cuts our pay by email.
fieldNote: Her **income is already shrinking** from rate cuts, so even a no-change world reads as pressure.
She blames the **platform's pay model**, not technology, and frames everything through the union.
A single bad week of **late flags** threatens her best routes, which shows how fragile the work is.

steps.text: Keep doing about 130 parcel drops a day on the morning routes
Put 50 a week aside to rebuild savings after the clutch repair
Go to the January depot meeting on the new per-drop rates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the app gets smarter and the vans stay the same for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the app already does the planning, so for drivers it's the same boss with a better brain. I'd warn people in the union chat that the next step is fewer of us on each route. I'd want a law that a person has to answer our complaints, not software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think they'll use the smarter routing to pile more drops on each of us and drop the rate again. The robots come slower, sure, but I've seen the little pavement robots in the city centre already. I'm not good with new apps, and if the job turns into managing gadgets I'll be the one who falls behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my routes and get onto the union's rates committee, which meets once a month. I'd keep saving 50 a week and not touch the cushion. I'd ask the union rep, Dave, whether there's a course they pay for, because I won't sign up for some random online thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit stubborn. I know I should learn the new stuff, but every time I open a new app I want to throw my phone in the canal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd fall behind. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Say the depot brings in a scanner that talks to a robot locker. The young lads would have it sorted in a day and I'd be the one ringing the help line. The app ranks us by speed, so slow means fewer routes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Noor that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm not panicking, we've got three months. Then I'd probably sit up looking at bus driver jobs with the council, because they have a union and a proper wage. Noor would laugh, because I always say I'll never drive a bus.

say: The app is the **same boss** with a better brain, and smarter routing will mean fewer drivers per route.
A **real person** should have to answer drivers' complaints, and I'd push the union to demand that in law.
think: Smarter routing will **pile more drops** on each of us and give the firm cover to cut the rate again.
I'm **slow with new apps**, so a job full of gadgets would push me down the speed rankings.
do: Join the union's **rates committee**, which meets once a month at the depot.
Keep saving **50 a week** and leave the three-month cushion untouched.
Ask the union rep about a **union-paid course** instead of trying random online training.
feel: **Uneasy and stubborn**, knowing she should learn new tools but hating every new app.
S1.quote: I know I should learn the new stuff, but every time I open a new app I want to throw my phone in the canal.
fieldNote: She sees **thinking AI** already in the app, so Steady Disruption is about workload and rate, not robots.
Her **resistance to new tech** is the real risk, and she knows it, which makes her quietly anxious.
The **bus driver idea** keeps returning: familiar driving, union wages, public employer.

steps.text: Join the union rates committee that meets monthly at the depot
Keep saving 50 a week and leave the cushion alone
Ask the union rep about a course the union pays for

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's next to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government that taxes the companies. If the firm can run on AI by 2028 and robots by 2031, the money should not all go to the shareholders. I'd be out at whatever protest the union called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my van job has about five years left in that picture. The app and the depot office go first, then around 2031 the vans drive themselves and robots carry the box to the door. I'm 27, so I'd be 32 with no trade and a driving licence nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for council bus driving in the first month, because it's a union job and I'd guess the public side changes slower. I'd cut my spending hard, no holidays, and push savings from three months to six. I'd also go to every union meeting about a transition fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Not panicked yet, because I can still drive for five years, but scared like when your stomach drops on a hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bus would change slower. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the council has to vote on things and the drivers have a strong union. I could be wrong, I don't really know. It just feels safer than a private app that can change everything with one update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Noor's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care work is people work, so I'd guess she's the last to go. That's funny, because she earns less than me. In that picture she'd be the steady one and I'd be the one looking.

say: Unions and **taxing the companies** matter more than ever if firms run on AI by 2028.
The gains from robots should not all go to **shareholders**, and I'd join any protest the union called.
think: My van job has about **five years left** before driverless vans and door robots arrive.
At 32 I'd have **no trade** and a driving licence that nobody needs any more.
do: Apply for **council bus driving** in the first month because it's unionised and public.
Cut spending hard and push savings from three to **six months**.
Attend every union meeting about a **transition fund** for drivers.
feel: **Scared**, with a dropping stomach, though not panicked while five years of driving remain.
S2.quote: I'm 27, so I'd be 32 with no trade and a driving licence nobody needs.
fieldNote: She grasps the **three-year gap**: the office goes in 2028, her van in about 2031.
Her plan leans on a **public union job**, which she admits is a guess.
She notes her partner's **lower-paid care work** may outlast her own, a reversal she finds strange.

steps.text: Apply for council bus driver jobs in the first month
Cancel holidays and cut takeaways and the phone plan
Build savings from three months up to six months
Attend union meetings on a transition fund for drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That sounds more like real life somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, louder: we need a plan for drivers before the vans drive themselves, not after. I'd say the government has five years, so no excuses. I'd sign every petition the union puts out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years for the thinking side and eight for robots means I'd be about 35 when the van goes. That's enough time to get onto the buses and maybe even become a trainer there. But I know myself, I'd put it off until the last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the buses within a year, not straight away, because I'd want to see the first vans running first. I'd keep saving 50 a week. I'd stay on the rates committee to fight for redundancy pay, because the app gives us nothing when it drops us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of breathing room. It's like seeing roadworks a mile ahead instead of round the corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put it off. What would make you actually move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first driverless van on my own route, honestly. Or Noor sitting me down with the laptop open on the council website. She's done that before with the dentist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friends who drive for the food apps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get a proper job with a contract while there are still openings. The food lads are on bikes, so maybe they get longer. I'd still tell them, because the app won't warn anyone.

say: The government has **five years**, so there's no excuse for having no plan for drivers.
I'd sign every **union petition** that asks for a driver plan before the vans drive themselves.
think: I'd be about **35** when the van goes, which is enough time to move onto the buses.
I know I'd **put it off** until the last year unless something forced my hand.
do: Apply for **bus driving** within a year, once the first driverless vans are on the road.
Fight on the rates committee for **redundancy pay** from the app.
feel: **Anxious** but with breathing room, like roadworks seen a mile ahead.
S3.quote: Five years for the thinking side and eight for robots means I'd be about 35 when the van goes.
fieldNote: More time turns her mood from alarm to **managed anxiety**, but also feeds her habit of **delay**.
She expects a **visible trigger**, a driverless van on her route, before she acts.
She looks out for **food-app riders**, showing a strong sense of solidarity.

steps.text: Apply for council bus driving within the first year
Keep saving 50 a week into the joint account
Push the rates committee for redundancy pay from the app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then robots in thirteen. I'd be nearly 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if governments use it, and a disaster if they waste it. I'd be on at the union to make a deal with the parcel firms now. Online I'd keep it simple: tax the robots, fund the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I might just keep driving for years and let it ride. Thirteen years till the robots is longer than I've been working. I'd probably be on the buses by then anyway, just because I'm sick of the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my routes for now and keep up the union work. Sometime in the next couple of years I'd move to the buses, mostly to get away from per-drop pay. I'd keep the three-month cushion and not do much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with uneasy. It's far enough off that I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might let it ride. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, if I'm honest. I don't like big changes, and ten years lets me tell myself it's fine. Noor would say that's exactly my problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the depot you'd worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, who's 58 and has driven parcels for 30 years. Ten years puts him at retirement, so he'd be all right. It's the lads my age who'd think they had forever.

say: Ten years is a **gift if used** and a disaster if governments waste it.
Online I'd keep it simple: **tax the robots** and fund the training.
think: Thirteen years until robots is longer than my **whole career** so far, so I might just let it ride.
I'd probably be **on the buses** by then anyway, just to escape per-drop pay.
do: Keep the **morning routes** and stay active in the union for now.
Move to **bus driving** within a couple of years to escape per-drop pay.
Hold the **three-month cushion** steady without big changes.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to sleep, because the change feels far off.
S4.quote: Thirteen years till the robots is longer than I've been working.
fieldNote: The decade of warning lets her **resistance** win: she'd mostly wait and drift.
Her move to the buses is driven by **app frustration**, not by AI.
She worries for **young drivers** who think they have forever, not for older colleagues.

steps.text: Keep driving the morning parcel routes for the next couple of years
Press the union to strike a deal with the parcel firms now
Switch to council bus driving within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years for the office and five for my van, and I'd be scrambling at 32 with no trade. What would help is a transition fund that pays drivers while we train, run with the unions, plus a guaranteed spot on the council buses for people who lose app work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Everyone talks about the robots like weather, but somebody at the parcel firm signs off on every cut. I'd like that person to ride with me for a day on Mill Lane with the broken lift.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about the robots like weather, but somebody at the parcel firm signs off on every cut.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old parcel van driver** paid per drop through an app, living with her girlfriend, a night care worker.
She is a committed **union member** who blames the platform's pay model, not technology itself.
She **avoids new apps** and admits her slowness with technology is her weak spot.
Her escape plan in every scenario is **council bus driving**, a familiar job with a union wage.
She is **anxious already** from rate cuts, alarmed by the two-year AGI picture, and drifts when given ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would leave her at 32 with no trade once driverless vans arrive.
whatWouldHelp: A union-run **transition fund** paying drivers while they train.
A **guaranteed place** on council buses for drivers who lose app work.
